rv.q: As a performer, Ms. Taylor also emerges from this two-hour pep rally smelling like a rose (a yellow one, let us say).
Taylor's Richards is a hoot yet she almost gets upstaged by another character, which is hard to do in a one-woman show.
The physical and spiritual illusion is so masterful that when a huge portrait of the real Richards appears at one point, it feels like a wasted effort.
Taylor lays her out there, warts and all, with relish and consummate skill.
Taylor is splendid, capturing the humor, decency, and abrasive energy in the woman while smoothly going from speech to phone call to more yakking.
In the end, the star outshines the star vehicle.
The best parts of the show come at the beginning and the end when Taylor is back at the front of the stage.
Just not enough of them to lasso our attention and really rope us in.
But a great dinner companion is not necessarily an ideal subject for a nearly two-hour play.

cn.t: Holland Taylor delivers a compelling performance as Texas Governor Ann Richards in this affectionate one-woman show, though critics find her acting outshines her uneven script, which struggles with structure despite capturing its subject's wit and charm.
